# Data Visualization With Power BI

Welcome to "Learn Data Visualization with Power BI"! In this course, you'll gain hands-on experience building visualizations, reports, and dashboards in Power BI – from simple charts to rich, shareable insights.

## Windows and Powershell

Unlike most Boot.dev courses, this one _requires_ that you use Windows. Power BI Desktop is unfortunately a Windows-only application.

> [!lane]
> You might be wondering, "Why not teach data visualization with a cross-platform or open-source tool?" Simply put, Power BI is the most popular business intelligence tool. Despite open-source being very popular among developers, business intelligence tools are still dominated by proprietary software.

## Eshopp

In this course we'll be building reports for a fictional e-commerce company: **Eshopp**. Eshopp sells all sorts of _super cool_ products online. You know, truly innovative stuff like "smart" toasters and "AI-powered" coffee mugs.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Ensure that you're on Windows.
2. [ ] Open [PowerShell](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/windows-powershell/starting-windows-powershell?view=powershell-7.5).
3. [ ] Install Golang and the Boot.dev CLI on Windows. Throughout this course, you'll be using the Boot.dev CLI to run our tests (which are just CLI commands) against your local environment. [Install it now](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev?tab=readme-ov-file#installation) if you don't have it already. All the instructions and troubleshooting info are in the readme on GitHub.
4. [ ] Verify the installation:

   ```sh
   bootdev --version
   ```

5. [ ] Once the `bootdev` command is working, log in and follow the instructions:
   ```sh
   bootdev login
   ```
6. [ ] Once you've installed the `bootdev` CLI and logged in, copy and paste the `submit` command from the right into your terminal and execute it.

> [!warning]
> You'll find each lesson's CLI commands in the test panel. `bootdev run <id>` runs checks without submitting. `bootdev run -s <id>` submits your work and marks the lesson complete when it passes.

# What Is Data Visualization?

![What is data visualization](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/what-is-data-visualization-1080x1920.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

[Data visualization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_and_information_visualization) is... exactly what it sounds like!

It's the process of representing data in visual formats like charts, graphs, and dashboards. It makes the information easier to understand and analyze, especially for busy executives who can't be bothered by tricky things like numbers and math.

Instead of your eyes glazing over staring at numbers in a table, a good visualization will help you to see patterns, trends, and outliers _at a glance_.

It's really about turning **data into insights**. A well-designed visual can communicate complex data quickly and clearly, helping decision-makers understand what's happening and why. You, as the data analyst, _create_ visuals, but who _uses_ them?

Most often, these visualizations focus on [key performance indicators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_indicator) (KPIs), which help different audiences understand how things are going:

1. **Executives and Managers:** Use dashboards to monitor company performance and make strategic decisions
2. **Business Teams (Sales, Marketing, Finance, HR):** Track key metrics, campaign results, or budgets in real time
3. **Clients and Stakeholders:** Understand reports and insights without needing to dig into raw data

create pretty graphs
call attention to real business insights

# What Is Power BI?

[Power BI](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-bi) is a data visualization and business intelligence tool from Microsoft, first released in 2015. It makes data analysis and reporting easier for everyone, not just technical experts.

We're using Power BI for this data visualization course because, as of 2025, it's _the_ [most popular BI tool](https://hginsights.com/resource/business-intelligence-market/) in the world.

![power bi](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/4yILqRx-1071x720.png)

> [!lane]
> ... but it _does_ mean we need to use Windows. ~~shudder~~.

> [!alex]
> Oh come on now, Windows is _fine_.

Windows is huge in the business intelligence, accounting, and finance world, so it makes sense that Power BI is too.

With Power BI, you can connect to data from many different sources, transform it, and create dashboards and reports that help you understand your data quickly. Power BI is best known for:

- Interactive dashboards
- Ease of use
- Integration within the rest of the Microsoft ecosystem
- Data connectivity
- Sharing and collaboration
- Automation

It gives you the tools to explore, understand, and share information confidently – all in one seamless, interactive platform. In our opinion it's the best tool for learning _real world_ data visualization skills.

Let's install Power BI Desktop on your machine!

## Assignment

There are three main ways to download and install Power BI Desktop, which is the free version of Power BI that we'll use in this course:

1. From the Microsoft Store (recommended)
   - [ ] Open the [Microsoft Store](https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9ntxr16hnw1t?hl=en-US&gl=US) app on your computer.
   - [ ] Search for `Power BI Desktop`.
   - [ ] Click **Get** or **Install** and let it download automatically.

   > [!tip]
   > This version updates automatically whenever a new release is available.

   ![install from microsoft store](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/w5zQqCt-761x720.png)

2. Via [WinGet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/package-manager/winget/), Windows' built-in package manager
   - [ ] Open PowerShell and run the following command:
     ```pwsh
     winget install --exact --id Microsoft.PowerBI --source winget
     ```
   - [ ] Enter `Y` to accept the license agreement if prompted.
   - [ ] Approve the administrator elevation prompt.
   - [ ] Wait for WinGet to report that Power BI was successfully installed.

3. From the Microsoft website
   - [ ] Go to the [Power BI Desktop product page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-bi/desktop).
   - [ ] Click "Advanced download options"; this should open a new page in the browser. (Clicking "Download now" would just launch the Microsoft Store.)
   - [ ] Select a language (preferably English) and click **Download** to grab the `.exe` file.
   - [ ] Run the downloaded executable and follow the on-screen installation steps.

   ![download power bi](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/LrghRQn-1280x600.png)

> [!warning]
> Only the Microsoft Store version updates automatically. If you install via WinGet or a manually downloaded `.exe`, Power BI will notify you when an update is available. WinGet users can also run `winget upgrade --exact --id Microsoft.PowerBI`.

Once Power BI is installed and you've verified that you can open the program, **submit** the CLI tests.

# UI Walkthrough

Before we start mucking around in earnest, it's important to understand the **Power BI Desktop interface**. Knowing where things are at a high level will make everything smoother down the line.

Power BI Desktop is made up of a few key areas:

- The **Ribbon**
- The **Report View**
- The **Data View** (also called the **Table View**)
- The **Model View**

Let's briefly go over each.

## 1. The Ribbon

![Power BI Ribbon](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/ldKkKfk-1280x363.png)

The Ribbon contains most of your primary tools, organized into tabs like _Home_, _Insert_, _Modeling_, and _View_.

> [!tip]
> Think of the Ribbon as your main control center – it's where almost every key feature begins.

## 2. The Report View

![Report View](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/IJHQnrR-1280x671.png)

The Report view is where you'll **build and design your visualizations**. The large canvas area in the center is where you drag and drop visuals to create a report.

The small icons on the very left-hand side under the Ribbon allow you to switch between views. The top one (with a report icon) is **Report view**.

> [!alex]
> This is where the magic happens! You'll spend most of your time here creating charts, visuals, and dashboards.

## 3. The Data View

![Data View](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/Wwnw2Qx-1280x632.png)

Directly below the Report view icon is the **Data view** – or, depending on the version of Power BI, the **Table view** (two names for the same thing). Here you can look directly at your dataset, similar to a spreadsheet. You can:

- Inspect rows and columns of your data
- Verify transformations
- Rename or reformat fields

> [!alex]
> This view helps you double-check that your raw data _is actually what you expect_ before you try to visualize it.

## 4. The Model View

![Data View](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/N8kGDjM-1280x613.png)

The bottom icon on the left is **Model view**, where you manage _relationships between tables_. You'll see your datasets as boxes connected by lines. Here you can:

- Create relationships manually
- Edit existing relationships
- See how your data models interact

> [!tip]
> If your visuals aren't displaying correctly, this is one of the first places to check. It's crucial to have all your relationships set up correctly for _any_ multi-table visualization.

# Creating a Report

Now that you're slightly familiar with the UI, let's create and save a new blank report in Power BI. This will be the report that we work on for the remainder of the course.

We won't load any data just yet, but it's important to make sure things are set up correctly.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Make a new directory somewhere on your computer for this course project. I put mine in my home folder and named it `dataviz-project`, but you can choose whatever location and name that you like.
2. [ ] Open Power BI Desktop and, before doing anything else, click `Options and settings` on the bottom left of the home page. Then go into `Options`, and select `Preview features` under `GLOBAL`. Ensure that the following three boxes are checked (they may be already):
   - "Power BI Project (.pbip) save option"
   - "Store semantic model using TMDL format"
   - "Store reports using enhanced metadata format (PBIR)"
3. [ ] If you had to change any of those settings, restart Power BI after clicking `OK` to save.

   ![pbip save options](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/Tumf09S-900x720.png)

   > [!danger]
   > These are relatively new features in Power BI, which are currently optional but will soon become the default. Our CLI tests will not work unless these features are enabled.

4. [ ] Back on the home page, click `Blank report` to create a new report.

   ![blank report](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/sM7nrnl-720x300.png)

5. [ ] With the new report open, click on `File` on the top left to show the Power BI home page again. Go back into `Options and settings` → `Options`. This time, go to `Regional Settings` under `CURRENT FILE`. Set "Locale for import" to `English (United States)`. This tells Power BI that, when importing data _into the current report only_, it should interpret dates, times, and numbers according to US conventions.

   ![locale for import](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/AIyzAP2-900x720.png)

   > [!info]
   > The sample datasets that we created for this course – which you'll download shortly – have numbers, dates, etc. in the US style. Fortunately, Power BI allows you to configure the locale on a per-report basis without changing your system settings.

6. [ ] Once the locale is set, save the report as `eshopp.pbip` (not the default `.pbix`!) in the directory you created for this course (`File` → `Save as` → etc.).
7. [ ] In PowerShell, `cd` into the course directory containing your saved project.

From the course directory, **submit** the CLI tests.

# Importing Data

Before we can start visualizing data, we need to _get our hands on some data_!

[CSV files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values) are simple text files that store data in a structured format, making them easy to read and write and _very_ common for exporting rows and columns of data from databases or spreadsheets. Let's download the CSVs that we'll be using throughout this course and import the first one into our Power BI project.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Download the [bundle of CSV files](https://storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/dataviz-csv.zip) – a ZIP archive – and extract its contents into the folder that you made for this course. Make sure you have _all seven_ CSV files at the root of the same directory where you saved `eshopp.pbip`.

It's time to actually _visualize_ Eshopp's sessions data!

## Assignment

1. [ ] In the Visualizations pane on the right-hand side of the Report view, click the Clustered Bar Chart icon. Resize the resulting chart to take up the full canvas (the dotted rectangle).

   ![clustered bar chart](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/1UJLnHP-369x413.png)

2. [ ] In the Data pane (all the way on the right), expand `customers`, then drag the `customer_payment_type` field to the Y-axis box under the Visualizations pane.

   > [!alex]

In this case, you'll probably see that it chooses `Sum` by default – but what we actually want is `Count (Distinct)`. That is, we want the X-axis to show the number of distinct customer IDs for each payment type. In order to change the aggregation, click the dropdown arrow next to `customer_id` in the X-axis box, and select `Count (Distinct)`.

lessons.title: Saving Reports
lessons.readme:
# Saving Reports

For most of this course we'll be using the `.pbip` (text-based) file format _because it's easier for the `bootdev` CLI to check_. However, the `.pbix` (Power BI Report File) binary file format is the standard for Power BI reports, and generally speaking is the better choice for data analysts working in GUI (graphical user interface) environments.

`.pbip` is a newer file format, introduced in 2023. It's mainly used by developers who want to store Power BI reports as text files so they're easy to track in version control (like Git).

It's important to note that the data files themselves (in our case the `.csv` files) are _not_ stored in the `.pbip` file. The `.pbip` file contains metadata about the data sources, transformations, and visualizations, but for your report to work, you _also_ need the original data files.

> [!danger]
> It's a _very good idea_ to save your work regularly, especially before making big changes. Power BI does **not** auto-save, so getting into the habit of saving often will help you avoid losing progress.

lessons.title: Data Types
lessons.readme:
# Data Types

Before we build more charts in Power BI, we need to understand **data types**. Data types tell Power BI what _kind_ of information each column contains – numbers, text, dates... you get the idea.

See, **the type of data determines the kind of visualizations you're allowed to create.** If Power BI doesn't know whether a value is text or a number, it can't decide how to group, sum, or compare it. Let's go over the most common data types.

![Data type explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/data-types-1080x1920.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

## 1. Text (or Strings)

Used for words, names, and labels – things that can't be added together. Things like:

- `Country`
- `Email`
- `Product Name`

You'll usually use text fields as **categories or labels** on your visuals, like the Y-axis of a bar chart or slices of a pie chart.

Text data is great for labeling visuals – but don't expect to run any math on it!

## 2. Whole Numbers

Used for numbers _without decimals_. For example:

- `Population`
- `Quantity Sold`
- `Number of Orders`

These are often **summed or counted** in charts to show totals or comparisons.

## 3. Decimal Numbers

Used for numeric values with decimals. For example:

- `Sale Quantity`
- `Product List Price`
- `Sale Discount`

You'll often visualize decimals with **bar charts, line graphs, or area charts** to show amounts or trends.

## 4. Date/Time

Used for anything that tracks time or dates. For example:

- `Order Date`
- `Year`
- `Timestamp`

Perfect for **line charts** or **time series** analysis – where you want to see how things change over time.

## 5. Boolean (True/False)

Used for yes/no or on/off data. For example:

- `Is Active`
- `Is Member`
- `Passed`

These fields can be used for **filters** or quick breakdowns, but they aren't typically plotted on charts directly.

lessons.readme:
# Bar and Column Charts

**Let's dig into some different types of charts!** Starting of course, with Bar Charts.

A Bar Chart displays data using horizontal bars. Each bar represents a category, and the length of the bar represents its value. Here's an example from a different data set:

![bar chart](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/yRuCVZc-1254x720.png)

## What Are Bar Charts Good For?

- Comparing total values between categories (e.g., Sales by Region, Revenue by Product Category)
- Highlighting differences across groups
- Showing rankings or proportions

> [!tip]
> Bar and column charts are great when you have a **category** (like region or product category) on one axis and a **numeric** value (like sale_quantity) on the other axis.

## Vertical vs. Horizontal

A column chart is just a bar chart with vertical bars instead of horizontal ones... hopefully that's obvious.

![column chart](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/Zve5Ywc-1280x672.png)

> [!alex]
> I prefer _bar_ charts (horizontal) when I have long category names or many items to compare. I prefer _column_ charts (vertical) when I have fewer categories and want to emphasize height rather than length.

lessons.title: Best Practices
lessons.readme:
# Best Practices

While many charts _technically work_ (the best kind of "work") for a given dataset, that doesn't mean all charts are a good fit.

- **Bar and Column Charts:** Compare categories
- **Line Charts:** Show change over time
- **Pie and Donut Charts:** Show proportions and percentages
- **Maps:** Visualize location-based data
- **Tables:** Display precise values when needed

> [!warning]
> Don't worry, we'll cover pie, donut, map, and table charts later.

Here are some of my rules of thumb for choosing the right chart and organizing them into useful reports.

## 1. Simplicity

- Use only the visuals you need to tell the story.
- Avoid unnecessary effects like 3D charts or shadows (looking at you, WordArt).
- Don't overload a single page with too many visuals – use multiple tabs if needed.
- Focus on one _key message_ per chart.
- If your audience can't understand the chart in 10 seconds, it's probably too complicated.

## 2. Consistency

- Keep font sizes, titles, and layouts uniform.
- Use the same capitalization and terminology across charts.
- Use consistent data formatting (e.g., all percentages or all currency).
- Don't mix unrelated chart types on the same report page.

## 3. Readability

- Ensure there's enough contrast between text and background.
- Avoid overlapping labels or tiny fonts.
- Keep spacing clean and even.

# Removing Duplicates

Duplicate rows can sneak into your dataset from joins, imports, or simple data entry errors. They can:

- Inflate totals or averages
- Create confusion in charts and tables
- Slow down refresh performance

Cleaning them ensures that every record represents a unique piece of data, so it's best to clean them up _early_ in Power Query.

## When to Remove Duplicates

I like to remove duplicates _after importing_ but before merging or appending any data. This keeps your transformations clean and avoids spreading duplicate data further down the pipeline.

## We Have Duplicate Data

Take a good look at our `sales.csv` data – it has duplicate rows! We have multiple rows with an id of `6`, and there are likely others besides! **Let's fix it!**

## Assignment

2. [ ] Select "Remove Duplicates."
   > [!warning]
   > When removing duplicates, make sure that column(s) you select truly identify a _unique_ record, otherwise, you might accidentally remove useful data.
3. [ ] Click "Close & Apply" in the ribbon to save your changes and close Power Query.

# Missing Values

Real-world data is ~~never~~ rarely perfect, and you'll often find missing or blank values. As a data analyst, it may fall to you to fill in the missing spots with something more meaningful.

Some entries are missing from the `website_sessions` data! Null values are strewn about the `session_quality_score` column. Let's replace those **null values** with `0.5`. Quality scores are from 0–1, so this will just assume the few missing values are "average." _How_ you should replace or handle missing data is very situation-dependent. Here we have less than 1% of the data missing, so this seems like an acceptable strategy.

> [!alex]
> Blanks in your data are like potholes – harmless at first, but they can trip you up later if you ignore them.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Open Power Query for the `website_sessions` query and select the `session_quality_score` column.
2. [ ] Go to the **Transform** tab.
3. [ ] Click **Replace Values**.
   - [ ] Enter "null" in the **Value to Find** box.
   - [ ] Enter `0.5` in the **Replace With** box.
     > [!danger]
     > On non-US English systems, you _may_ need to enter `0,5` instead of `0.5` if your locale uses a comma as the decimal separator.
   - [ ] Click **OK**.

   > [!alex]
   > For text data it often makes sense to use a placeholder string like: `Unknown`, `Missing`, or `N/A`; just be consistent. It's trickier with numbers. Sometimes you can use a representative value, like an average or median, sometimes you can leave it `null`, and sometimes it's best to just remove erroneous nulls.

4. [ ] Close & Apply the query.

lessons.title: Performance Considerations
lessons.readme:
# Performance Considerations

As your datasets grow, Power Query transformations can start to slow down, but there are ways to make queries run faster and data refreshes smoother.

> [!alex]
> A fast Power Query setup means less waiting and more analyzing – which is what we actually want to spend our time doing.

## Keep Only What You Need

The more data you load, the slower your queries become. Try to:

- Remove unnecessary columns early.
- Filter out rows you don't need before applying other steps.
- Avoid loading large intermediate tables that aren't used in visuals.

## Minimize Complex Steps

Every transformation adds work for Power Query to process. Combine simple steps instead of stacking many small ones, and avoid transformations that recalculate the same data multiple times.

> [!alex]
> Fewer steps = faster queries

## Watch Out for Data Type Changes

Changing data types repeatedly can slow things down. Set the correct types once, ideally right after loading your data.

# Filters

Formatting improves how your charts _look_, while filters control _what data they display_. They're perfect for slicing the data _at view time_ into specific regions, time periods, or categories without changing your dataset or power query transformations.

There are three main types of filters in Power BI, and they're shown in the "Filters" pane to the left of the "Visualizations" pane.

1. **Visual-Level Filters:** Affect only the selected chart
2. **Page-Level Filters:** Affect all visuals on the same page
3. **Report-Level Filters:** Affect every page in the entire report

> [!alex]
> I use filters depending on who is using this dashboard/visualization. Do they need all the data? Will they want to filter on something specific? Then I'll add whichever filter I need.

## Assignment

# Star Schema

![Star Schema Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/Star-Schema-1080x1920.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

A [star schema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_schema) organizes your model into one central _fact table_ (sales) surrounded by _dimension tables_. It's the simplest, most performant shape for analytic reporting in Power BI.

- Fact (many rows): `sales`
- Dimensions (unique keys): `dates`, `products`, `customers`, `stores`

![model view](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/1JabbBi-900x720.png)

This setup allows us to answer questions like:

- "What were the total sales _for each product_ in a given _month_?"
- "How many _customers_ bought _products_ in a specific _store_?"
- "What was the _average sale amount_ for _each customer_ in a given _year_?"

> [!alex]
> Facts = "what happened" (sales)
>
> Dimensions = "about what" (by product, date, customer, store, etc)

## Assignment

1. [ ] Import the following CSVs (Get Data → Text/CSV):
   - [ ] `dates.csv`
   - [ ] `products.csv`
   - [ ] `stores.csv`

3. [ ] Open the "Model View" – it's below "Report" and "Table" views on the left hand side.
4. [ ] Drag the boxes so that `products`, `customers`, `stores`, and `dates` (dimension tables) are all the spokes of the star. The sales (fact) table should be in the middle. The `website_sessions` should be off to the side, connected to both `stores` and `customers`.

> [!info]
> The `sales` and `website_sessions` tables _should_ have lines connecting to the other tables automatically. Power BI is smart enough to recognize the ID columns. If it doesn't, you can add relationships manually by dragging the ID column from one table to the matching ID column in another table.

# Measures

Calculated columns and measures both perform calculations, but they're quite different.

A "calculated column" is stored in your model and evaluated _for each row_ in a table. A "measure" is calculated on the fly as a **total**, updating _dynamically_ as you interact with your report.

lessons.readme:
# Cardinality and Cross Filters

Cardinality (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many) describes the type of relationship between two tables.

When looking at the Model View we can actually _see_ the cardinality represented visually:

![direction](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/b3y7tbi-815x688.png)

This diagram shows a standard one-to-many relationship between `products` (`1`) and `sales` (`*`).

When you right-click on a relationship and click "properties" you'll see a more detailed view:

![cardinality](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/VHzeyaA-644x720.png)

> [!alex]  
> For _most_ data models, you'll use many-to-one or one-to-many relationships. Many-to-many and _especially_ one-to-one are more rare.

## Note: Cross Filter Direction

In the properties pane, there's a setting that controls how filters move between the two tables.

![filters](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/PPINI0p-1071x720.png)

- _Single_ (recommended) means the filter flows from the one side into the many side
- _Both_ allows filters to move in both directions

Imagine a `Schools` table (one) related to a `Students` table (many), and that "Lakeside High" happens to not have any students before the year 2012. Here's how single and both direction filtering would work:

| Filter                         | Single Direction                                | Both Directions                                      |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Schools to "Lakeside High"** | Students are filtered to Lakeside High students | Students are filtered to Lakeside High students      |
| **Students to "Before 2012"**  | Schools table is unaffected (good)              | "Lakeside High" is filtered from schools table (bad) |

It feels strange that filtering students affects the schools table, and that rule of thumb applies to most scenarios.

> [!alex]  
> In my 5+ years of using Power BI I've only used "Both" a handful of times.

answers: One-to-one
One-to-many (or many-to-one)
Many-to-many

questions.question: Why is 'Single' _usually_ better for cross filtering than 'Both'?
answers: It prevents unexpected filtering of the 'one' side
It prevents unexpected filtering of the 'many' side
questions.answer: It prevents unexpected filtering of the 'one' side

lessons.title: DAX

# DAX

[DAX](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/) stands for **Data Analysis Expressions**. It's the language that Power BI uses to perform calculations, build metrics, and create dynamic insights in your reports. While it looks a bit like Excel, DAX is designed specifically for analytical models and large datasets.

DAX allows you to create things like totals, averages, percentages, comparisons, KPIs, and time-based calculations that react instantly to slicers and filters in your report. Any time you see a number in a Power BI visual that updates when you click something, DAX is doing the work behind the scenes.

> [!tip]
> The formulas we wrote in the last chapter were _simple_ DAX expressions.

There are two main places where you can write DAX in Power BI:

- The formula input that we used for calculated columns and measures
- The DAX query view

![DAX video](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/Dax_V41-1080x1882.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

## DAX Query View

The [DAX query view](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/transform-model/dax-query-view) is a more advanced area where you can write DAX queries to inspect data, test expressions, and debug calculations. It's especially helpful when you want to see exactly what a DAX expression is returning without building a full visual.

> [!alex]
> Query View is the easiest way to "peek behind the curtain" of your model.

You can open it from the left-hand pane:

![query view](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/1sDWIXm-1280x620.png)

### Select Columns

This query uses the [`SELECTCOLUMNS`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/SELECTCOLUMNS-function-dax) function to create a new table with only the columns we specify. It lets us get a quick view into our data – it's a bit like running a one-off SQL `SELECT` statement.

```text
EVALUATE
SELECTCOLUMNS(
    sales,
    "sale_price", sales[price],
    "customer_id", sales[customer_id]
)
```

> [!info]
> The [`EVALUATE`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/evaluate-statement-dax) statement simply tells DAX to run the query and return the results as a table.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Open the DAX query view. It's right below the Model view on the left-hand side of the screen.
2. [ ] Write a query that selects the `customer_name` and `customer_age` columns from the `customers` table.
3. [ ] Run your query by clicking the "Run" button. It should output a simple table in results section below.

Save the project and, from the course directory, **submit** the CLI tests.

# Logical Functions – IF

[Logical functions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/logical-functions-dax) let your DAX formulas make decisions based on conditions. With them you can label rows, create flags, or change calculations depending on your data.

In the sales dataset, we might want to mark which orders are bulk orders, or whether a sale has a discount applied. Logical functions like [`IF`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/if-function-dax) and [`SWITCH`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/switch-function-dax) are perfect for this.

> [!alex]
> Logical functions turn your numbers into rules the business actually cares about.

You will typically use logical functions in:

- Calculated columns, for row-by-row labels
- Measures, for dynamic classification based on filters

## IF Function

The [`IF`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/if-function-dax) function checks a condition and returns one value if true, another if false. Here's an example of an `IF` function that labels homes as "Jumbo" or "Normal" based on whether their price is above $700,000:

```text
HouseType = IF(Homes[Price] > 700000, "Jumbo", "Normal")
```

Notice that it has 3 parameters:

- **Logical Test:** The condition to check (e.g., `Homes[Price] > 700000`)
- **Value if True:** What to return if the condition is true (e.g., `"Jumbo"`)
- **Value if False:** What to return if the condition is false (e.g., `"Normal"`)

and returns the value as `HouseType`.

## Assignment

2. [ ] Look over some of the values in the new column to ensure the function is working as expected.

# SWITCH Function

The [`SWITCH`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/switch-function-dax) function is like a more powerful `IF`. It checks multiple conditions and returns different values based on which condition is true. Here's an example that classifies homes into "Small," "Medium," or "Large" based on the `SquareFeet` column:

```text
OrderSize =
SWITCH(
   TRUE,
   Homes[SquareFeet] <= 2000, "Small",
   Homes[SquareFeet] <= 3000, "Medium",
   "Large"
)
```

> [!tip]
> You might be wondering, "Why the `TRUE` at the beginning of the `SWITCH` function?" It's a bit odd, and it usually will just be `TRUE`, but it's specified because you _can_ change it. It's just the value that the following conditions need to match. In this case `Homes[SquareFeet] <= 2000` and `Homes[SquareFeet] <= 3000` need to evaluate to `TRUE` to return their respective "Small" and "Medium" values.

## Assignment

lessons.title: Time Intelligence Functions
lessons.readme:
# Time Intelligence Functions

Time functions in DAX help you analyze how values change over time by using your Date table to understand the order of days, months, and years. Two of my favorites are:

## Total Month-to-Date

The [`TOTALMTD`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/totalmtd-function-dax) function calculates the total of a measure from the start of the current month up to the current date. Here's an example that calculates the number of new customers acquired in the current month up to today.

```text
MTD New Customers =
  TOTALMTD(
    [New Customers],
    dates[date]
  )
```

## Previous Month

The [`PREVIOUSMONTH`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/previousmonth-function-dax) function shifts the date context back one full month and calculates the measure for that previous month. Here's an example that calculates the number of new customers acquired in the previous month:

```text
Previous Month New Customers =
  CALCULATE(
    [New Customers],
    PREVIOUSMONTH(dates[date])
  )
```

> [!alex]
> I've used these functions for years, and you'll see them used in a lot of dashboards! Now, because _our_ data for this course is a snapshot from the past, we won't use these now, but when you have "live" data they're very useful.

lessons.readme:
# More Time Functions

Before we move on, it's worth mentioning some other particularly useful time functions:

- [`TOTALYTD`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/totalytd-function-dax): Calculates year-to-date values. Useful for tracking annual performance and cumulative growth.
- [`DATEADD`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/dateadd-function-dax): Shifts the date context by a number of days, months, quarters, or years. Perfect for week-over-week or month-over-month comparisons.
- [`DATESINPERIOD`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/datesinperiod-function-dax): Returns a rolling range of dates. Essential for things like rolling 7-day, 30-day, or 90-day performance.
- [`DATEDIFF`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/datediff-function-dax): Calculates the difference between two dates in days, months, or years. Great for calculating age, tenure, or time to complete tasks.
- [`DATE`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/date-function-dax): Creates a date from year, month, and day values. Useful for constructing specific dates in your data model.
- [`TODAY`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/today-function-dax): Returns the current date. Handy for dynamic reports that need to show today's data.

> [!alex]
> If you learn these, you can build almost every core time-based metric.

For a more complete list, [check the docs here](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/date-and-time-functions-dax).

## Example of Dates in Period

```text
num_sales_in_2026 =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( sales[sale_quantity] ),
    DATESINPERIOD ( dates[date], DATE( 2026, 01, 01 ), 1, YEAR )
)
```

- `dates[date]` is a reference to a column containing date values that have a relationship that ties back to our `sales`
- `DATE( 2026, 01, 01 )` is the start date
- `1` is the number of intervals
- `YEAR` is the interval duration

## Assignment

   > [!tip]
   > Use `CALCULATE` with `[total_revenue]` as its first argument – measures are referenced directly, not wrapped in `SUM()`.
2. [ ] Add the `revenue_in_feb` measure to your multi-value card.

# Add Columns

We've used the `SELECTCOLUMNS` function in the DAX query view to _return specific columns_ from our table. The [`ADDCOLUMNS`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/ADDCOLUMNS-function-dax) function returns the columns we specify _as well as all the original_ columns.

This returns all the original `sales` columns, as well as a new column called `discounted_quantity`:

```text
EVALUATE
ADDCOLUMNS(
  sales,
  "discounted_quantity", sales[sale_quantity] * (1 - sales[sale_discount])
)
```

## Related Data

When using a function like `SELECTCOLUMNS` or `ADDCOLUMNS`, you can't reference a related table directly. To do so, you need to use the `RELATED` function:

```text
EVALUATE
SELECTCOLUMNS(
    users,
    "user_name", users[name],
    "user_server", RELATED('servers'[name]),
    "user_created_at", RELATED('dates'[created_at])
)
```

## Order By

You can order the data in a DAX expression with the `ORDER BY` keywords:

```text
EVALUATE
SELECTCOLUMNS(
    users,
    "user_name", users[name],
    "user_server", RELATED('servers'[name]),
    "user_created_at", RELATED('dates'[created_at])
)
ORDER BY
    [user_created_at] DESC
```

   You'll want to use these functions:
   - [`DATEDIFF`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/datediff-function-dax): Calculates the difference between two dates in days, months, or years. Great for calculating age, tenure, or time to complete tasks.
   - [`DATE`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/date-function-dax): Creates a date from year, month, and day values. Useful for constructing specific dates in your data model.

3. [ ] Order the results by the days before migration column, descending.

lessons.readme:
# Aggregations

[Aggregation functions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/aggregation-functions-dax) in DAX aggregate a result from _multiple rows_ in a column. These are super common DAX functions, and they form the foundation for almost every measure you'll write.

> [!alex]
> Aggregators answer "How much?", "How many?", or "What's the average?" for a column.

We've already used some of these, but let's cover more of the most common functions in a bit more detail.

## Sum

The [`SUM`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/sum-function-dax) function adds all values in a column.

```text
Total Quantity = SUM(sales[sale_quantity])
```

## Average

The [`AVERAGE`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/average-function-dax) function calculates the mean value of a column.

```text
Average Discount = AVERAGE(sales[sale_discount])
```

## Count

The [`COUNT`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/count-function-dax) function counts the number of rows that contain a value in a column.

```text
Total Sales = COUNT(sales[sale_id])
```

## Min

The [`MIN`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/min-function-dax) function returns the smallest value in a column.

```text
Minimum Quantity = MIN(sales[sale_quantity])
```

## Max

The [`MAX`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/max-function-dax) function returns the largest value in a column.

```text
Maximum Quantity = MAX(sales[sale_quantity])
```

lessons.readme:
# Aggregations As Measures

A common mistake in DAX is using aggregators like `SUM` in calculated columns instead of measures. **Don't do that!** It will return the same number on every row because calculated columns are row-by-row, not a single value for the whole table.

![as column](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/I4HSBCi-1165x720.png)

This means:

- It doesn't respond to filters.
- It takes up storage in your model.
- It behaves incorrectly in visuals.

> [!alex]
> A `SUM` in a calculated column is almost never what you want.

Instead, **use a measure** for aggregations! A _measure_ is a single value that recalculates dynamically based on the current filter context. This means it:

- Changes when you slice by date, customer, or product
- Returns different values depending on the visual
- Uses no extra storage
- Reflects how much was sold in the _filtered_ context

> [!alex]
> Measures think in totals; columns think row-by-row. An aggregator like `SUM` belongs in a measure.

lessons.title: Iterators
lessons.readme:
# Iterators

Iterator functions in DAX evaluate an expression row-by-row, _then_ aggregate the results. They allow you to define what should happen in each row before summing, averaging, or comparing.

> [!alex]
> Aggregators look at a column, while iterators look at each row first.

Let's cover some of the most common functions.

## SumX

The [`SUMX`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/sumx-function-dax) function iterates over a table, evaluating an expression for each row, then sums the results.

```text
Total Sales Value = SUMX(
    sales,
    sales[sale_quantity] * RELATED(products[product_list_price])
)
```

> [!info]  
> `RELATED` lets us access the `product_list_price` column from the `products` table, even though this formula is in the `sales` table. This works because the `sales` and `products` tables have a _relationship_ – they both have a `product_id` column. Power BI can often detect such relationships automatically.

## AverageX

The [`AVERAGEX`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/averagex-function-dax) function works similarly, but averages the results instead of summing them.

```text
Average Sales Value = AVERAGEX(
    sales,
    sales[sale_quantity] * RELATED(products[product_list_price])
)
```

## MinX

The [`MINX`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/minx-function-dax) function finds the _minimum_ value of an expression evaluated over a table.

```text
Min Product Cost = MINX(
    products,
    products[product_standard_cost]
)
```

## MaxX

The [`MAXX`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dax/maxx-function-dax) function finds the _maximum_ value of an expression evaluated over a table.

```text
Max Product Cost = MAXX(
    products,
    products[product_standard_cost]
)
```

> [!tip]
> Iterator function names always end with **X**.

# Calculated Columns vs. Measures

Iterators are a type of aggregator, so you almost always want to use them in a **measure** rather than a **calculated column**.

> [!alex]
> It's tempting to use an iterator in a calculated column because the math is done row-by-row _initially_, but it still needs to properly aggregate at the end, so it should be a measure.

Here's a table showing the difference between a calculated column and a measure using the `SUMX` iterator:

![don't use iterators on columns](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/9skR9Vv-631x720.png)

Measure responds to slicers, filters, and drilldowns. The column never changes.

So, just like aggregations, **iterators belong on measures**!

answers: Measures aggregate dynamically and respond to filters, slicers, and drilldowns
Calculated columns perform less work during aggregation
Calculated columns automatically respond to slicers and visuals

lessons.title: Context in DAX
lessons.readme:
# Context in DAX

Context is one of the most important concepts in DAX. It determines how a DAX expression is evaluated and which rows are included in the calculation.

There are two types of context you must understand: Row Context and Filter Context.

- Row context tells DAX "evaluate this row."
- Filter context tells DAX "evaluate these filtered rows."

## Row Context in DAX

Row context exists when DAX evaluates a formula **for each row of a table**. You get row context in DAX when you:

- Create a calculated column
- Use iterators like `SUMX`, `AVERAGEX`, `MINX`, `MAXX`
- Use `ADDCOLUMNS`

Example in a calculated column:

```text
Revenue Column = sales[sale_quantity] * RELATED(products[product_list_price])
```

DAX evaluates this expression for _each individual row_. No slicers or visuals can change this value, because row context is created at model-processing time.

Row context = DAX evaluating expressions row-by-row.

## Filter Context in DAX

Filter context exists when DAX evaluates a measure using only the rows allowed by filters.

Filter context is created by:

- Visual filters
- Slicers
- Page/report/visual-level filters
- Relationship filtering between tables
- The `CALCULATE` function (which can modify filter context)

Example measure:

```text
Total Quantity = SUM(sales[sale_quantity])
```

When DAX runs this measure, it applies all active filters – from visuals, slicers, relationships, `CALCULATE`, etc. Then it sums the Quantity column only for the rows in the filtered set.

Filter context = DAX evaluating expressions using the currently filtered rows.

# Pie Charts

A [pie chart](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-pie-donut-chart?tabs=powerbi-desktop) represents data as slices of a circle, showing proportions of a whole. Each slice represents a category's share of the total.

![pie chart](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/zLIT4Bv-1280x642.png)

Pie charts work best when you have a small number of categories (ideally 5 or fewer) and want to show how each part contributes to the whole.

> [!alex]
> Pie charts get a bad rap in the data viz community, but they're perfectly fine for simple proportions. Just don't use them for comparing similar-sized slices – that's where they fall apart.

## When to Use Pie Charts

- Showing market share or revenue split
- Displaying category breakdowns (like sales by store type)
- Visualizing budget allocations

## When NOT to Use Pie Charts

- When you have more than 5–6 categories
- When slices are nearly the same size (hard to compare)
- When you need precise comparisons (use a bar chart instead)

# Donut Charts

A [donut chart](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-pie-donut-chart?tabs=powerbi-desktop) is essentially a pie chart with a hole in the middle. That's it. Really.

## Pie vs. Donut

The choice between pie and donut is mostly aesthetic. Some people find donuts easier to read because the focus shifts to the arc lengths rather than the angles. Others just think they look more modern.

Use whichever fits your dashboard's style better – just be consistent across your report.

- Use 5 or fewer categories for readability
- Make sure the measure represents parts of a whole

# Area Charts

[Area charts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-basic-area-chart) are just like line charts, but with the space below the line filled in. This shading emphasizes the volume or magnitude of values over time.

![area chart](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/VAtFeql-1280x652.png)

> [!alex]
> Area charts answer the question, "How is this metric trending over time, and how _much_ of it is there?"

## When to Use Area Charts

- Showing cumulative totals over time
- Emphasizing the magnitude of change (not just direction)

# Scatterplots

[Scatterplots](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-scatter) help you explore the **relationship between two numeric values**. Each point represents a single record, plotted by its X and Y values.

They're perfect for spotting correlations, clusters, and outliers in your data.

> [!alex]
> I use scatterplots constantly for two things: finding trends between variables, and catching outliers that might indicate bad data.

![scatterplot with trend line](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/VQHXHft-1280x638.png)

## Correlations

When points trend upward from left to right, you have a **positive correlation** – as one value increases, so does the other. In our website sessions data, we'd expect longer sessions to have more pages visited.

When points trend downward, you have a **negative correlation**. And when points are scattered randomly, there's no correlation at all.

## Trend Lines

Adding a trend line makes correlations easier to see. Power BI can calculate and display this line automatically through the Analytics pane.

> [!tip]
> Look for points that fall far from the trend line – these outliers might be data entry errors or genuinely unusual records worth investigating.

# Waterfall Charts

[Waterfall charts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-waterfall-charts?tabs=powerbi-desktop) show how a total is built up or broken down across categories. Each bar represents an increase or decrease, with the final bar showing the total.

![waterfall](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/unLQOUn-914x597.png)

They're perfect for explaining "Where did this total come from?" or "What contributed to this change?"

> [!alex]
> Waterfall charts are fantastic for financial reporting. They make it easy to see which categories are driving growth or dragging down performance.

## Reading a Waterfall Chart

- **Green bars** represent increases (positive contributions)
- **Red bars** represent decreases (negative contributions)
- **Blue bar** at the end shows the running total

The visual tells a story: start at zero, add or subtract each category's contribution, and end at the final total.

## When to Use Waterfall Charts

- Breaking down revenue by product category
- Showing profit and loss by department
- Explaining budget variances
- Visualizing how different factors contribute to a final result

# Ribbon Charts

[Ribbon charts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/desktop-ribbon-charts?tabs=powerbi-desktop) show how categories change **rank** over time. The "ribbons" connect each category across time periods, making it easy to see which ones rise or fall in position.

> [!alex]
> Ribbon charts are awesome for competitive analysis. Which product category is winning this month? Which one is losing ground? The ribbons make it instantly obvious.

## When to Use Ribbon Charts

- Tracking market share rankings over time
- Showing which products/regions move up or down
- Visualizing competitive positioning changes
- Any scenario where **relative rank** matters more than absolute values

## Reading a Ribbon Chart

- Categories are stacked by their value (highest on top)
- Ribbons show how each category moves between time periods
- Crossing ribbons indicate a change in ranking
- The width of each ribbon represents the value

# Combo Charts

[Combo charts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/visuals/power-bi-visualization-combo-chart?tabs=powerbi-desktop) combine two chart types – typically bars and a line – in a single visual. They're useful when you want to compare two related metrics that have different scales or units.

> [!alex]
> Combo charts are perfect when one measure might relate to the other. For example: "When discounts are higher, do sales go up?"

## When to Use Combo Charts

- Comparing volume (bars) against a rate or percentage (line)
- Showing sales quantity alongside average discount
- Displaying revenue with profit margin trend
- Any time two metrics tell a better story together

## Tips for Effective Combo Charts

- Use bars for the "main" metric and lines for the supporting metric
- Make sure the two metrics are actually related
- Don't overload – two measures is usually the sweet spot
- Consider using different colors to clearly distinguish the bar from the line

> [!warning]
> Combo charts can get confusing if the two metrics aren't related. If viewers have to think hard about the connection, consider using two separate charts instead.

lessons.readme:
# My Top 3 Most Useful Charts

Power BI offers dozens of chart types, but in practice, most dashboards rely on just a handful of visuals that consistently communicate information clearly.

> [!alex]
> Simple charts get used. Complicated charts get ignored.

![Favorite Charts](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/favorite-charts-1080x1920.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

Here are the three chart types I use most often in real-world dashboards.

## 1. Bar Charts

Bar charts are the most versatile and widely used chart type. They're best for comparing values across categories.

Common use cases:

- Sales by region
- Revenue by product
- Customers by segment

Bar charts make it easy to see differences at a glance and are intuitive for almost everyone viewing a dashboard.

## 2. Line Charts

Line charts are the best choice for time-based data. They show trends, growth, and changes over time.

Common use cases:

- Monthly revenue trends
- Daily website traffic
- Year-over-year performance

Line charts help viewers understand direction and movement, not just individual values.

## 3. Cards and KPIs

Cards and KPI visuals highlight important numbers. They're best for totals, averages, percentages, and key performance indicators.

Common use cases:

- Total revenue
- Customer count
- Conversion rate
- Year-to-date sales

These visuals are usually placed at the top of a dashboard to immediately communicate the most important metrics.

## Why These Charts Matter

These three chart types cover most real-world dashboard needs:

- **Bar charts** for comparing categories
- **Line charts** for tracking performance over time
- **Cards** for highlighting key metrics quickly

If you master these charts, you can build clear and effective dashboards without relying on overly complex visuals. The fancier chart types we covered in this chapter are useful in specific situations, but these three are your bread and butter.

> [!alex]
> When in doubt, use a bar chart. Seriously.

answers: Tree maps, gauges, and decomposition trees
Scatter plots, radar charts, and waterfall charts

questions.answer: Bar charts, line charts, and cards/KPIs

lessons.readme:
# Hierarchies and Drill Downs

Hierarchies let you organize data into natural levels, like:

```text
Country → State → City
```

Drill downs then let you navigate between these levels inside a visual, making reports interactive and explorable.

> [!alex]
> Hierarchies make your visuals feel alive. Click, explore, drill into the data. Your stakeholders will think you're a wizard.

## Creating a Hierarchy

A hierarchy is simply a grouping of related fields in a specific order – from broadest to most specific. Power BI lets you create hierarchies by nesting fields together in the Data pane.

Once created, you can use the hierarchy in any visual that supports drill downs, like bar charts, column charts, or tables.

## Drill Down Features

Power BI gives you three ways to explore your hierarchy:

1. **Drill Down** – Move one level deeper (e.g., Country → State)
2. **Drill Up** – Go back up a level (e.g., State → Country)
3. **Expand All** – Show multiple levels at once

You can access these by right-clicking on a data point or using the drill icons in the visual header.

![drill down menu](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/9huQyqL-1280x647.png)

> [!tip]
> Drill downs are one of the easiest ways to impress stakeholders. They love clicking around and exploring the data themselves!

## Assignment

1. [ ] Import the `geographies.csv` file into Power BI. This is some _third party_ research data that we've acquired to better understand population density in areas of interest.
2. [ ] In the Data pane on the right, create a hierarchy from the geography fields: right-click `geography_country` → Create hierarchy, then drag or right-click to add `geography_state` and `geography_city` to it (in that order).
   > [!warning]
   > The order matters! Make sure country is at the top, then state, then city. If you add them in the wrong order, you can drag them to rearrange within the hierarchy.
3. [ ] Create a new page (Page 8) and rename it "Geo"
4. [ ] Insert a Clustered Column Chart spanning the full page
5. [ ] Set `geography_population` as the Y-axis
6. [ ] Set your `geography_country Hierarchy` as the X-axis
7. [ ] At the top of the chart, turn on drill-down ability, then use the forked "Expand all down one level" arrow to show the hierarchy levels together.

   You should start by seeing the lowest drilled down view (a bunch of bars, one for each city). Click the up arrow at the top of the chart to "drill up", and on an individual category to drill down. Play with it until you understand the mechanics.

8. [ ] Format the title: General → Title → Text → "Population by Geography"

# Dashboard Design Principles

![Design Principles Explainer Video](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/6_Data_Visualization-1080x1920.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

Dashboards are usually the first thing people see. Managers rarely dig into reports or tables like an analyst would. They open a dashboard, glance at it for a minute or two, and decide what to do next.

That means your job is _not_ to show everything. Your job is to _make the important stuff obvious_.

> [!alex]
> When dashboards fail, it's usually not because the data is wrong, but because the message is unclear.

Before touching charts or formatting, you should think about the goal of the dashboard. Who is this for? What decisions should it help them make?

## Core Design Principles

The following principles apply to almost every effective dashboard.

### Start With One Clear Question

Every dashboard should answer a small number of questions, not everything at once. Examples:

- How are sales performing this month?
- Where are we losing customers?
- Which regions need attention?

If a visual doesn't help answer the main question, it probably doesn't belong on the dashboard.

### Use Visual Hierarchy

Not all information is equally important. Good hierarchy usually looks like this:

- [KPIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_indicator) at the top
- Primary charts in the center
- Supporting details below or to the side

Your eye should naturally move from the most important insight to the least important one.

### Keep It Simple

Clutter makes dashboards harder to read. Common problems:

- Too many colors
- Too many charts
- Too much text

White space is helpful! It separates ideas and makes insights easier to spot.

> [!alex]
> If you need to explain how to read your dashboard, it's probably too complicated.

### Be Consistent

Consistency builds trust and makes dashboards easier to use. Try to keep:

- The same colors representing the same metrics
- The same font sizes for similar visuals
- The same chart types for the same kinds of data

lessons.readme:
# Choosing the Right Chart

Picking a chart is one of the easiest ways to make or break a dashboard. You can have clean data and a nice layout, but if the chart type is wrong, the insight gets lost – or at least misunderstood.

The goal is not to use fancy visuals. The goal is to make the data easy to understand at a glance.

## Common Chart Use Cases

Different questions require different chart types. Here are the most common ones you'll use in Power BI.

### Comparing Values

When you want to compare numbers across categories, simple charts work best. Good options:

- Bar charts
- Column charts

Examples:

- Sales by region
- Customers by plan type
- Revenue by product

Bar charts are usually easier to read when you have long category names.

### Showing Trends Over Time

When time is involved, you almost always want a line chart. Good options:

- Line charts
- Area charts

Examples:

- Monthly sales
- Daily website traffic
- Year-over-year growth

> [!alex]
> I've seen people use bar charts for time series, but it can get very congested with larger date ranges. I personally don't use them for time series at all.

### Showing Parts of a Whole

Use these when you want to show how something breaks down into pieces. Good options:

- Stacked bar charts
- Stacked column charts

Use pie or donut charts sparingly. They're best for very simple comparisons with only a few categories.

> [!alex]
> If your pie chart needs a legend, it probably should not be a pie chart.

### Showing Relationships

When you want to see how two numbers move together, use charts designed for comparison. Good options:

- Scatter plots
- Bubble charts

Examples:

- Price vs. sales volume
- Marketing spend vs. conversions

These charts are great for spotting patterns and outliers.

## Assignment

Let's create a CEO Dashboard that applies some of these "dashboard best practices." For now, let's just pick a theme and get the right charts and components on there.

1. [ ] Create a new page and name it `CEO Dashboard`.
2. [ ] Go to Design → Themes and select the "Frontier" theme (it will apply to all pages, that's okay).
3. [ ] Add the following charts/components to the page; don't worry about position and formatting yet.
   - [ ] A "CEO Dashboard" text box in the top-left corner: Insert → Text box
   - [ ] A card (always use the "new" kind with the lightning bolt on the icon) that displays total revenue
   - [ ] Another card that displays the total units sold
   - [ ] A Stacked Area Chart (_not_ "100% Stacked Area Chart") that shows revenue – the sum of `discounted_price` – over time, by **month** by product category
     > [!tip]
     > On the X-axis, use the `date` hierarchy and keep Year, Quarter, and Month, but _remove_ Day. Starting at Year, click the forked arrow ("Expand all down one level") _twice_ to show months grouped by year.
   - [ ] A Clustered Column Chart that shows the sum of session durations by store name
   - [ ] A Clustered Column Chart that shows the **quantity of sales** (count of sale IDs) by product brand
   - [ ] A donut chart that shows population by country at the highest level and _can drill down_

lessons.title: Telling Stories With Data
lessons.readme:
# Telling Stories With Data

Dashboards are not just collections of charts; they're stories. Each visual should help guide someone from a question to an insight and then to an action.

If charts are placed randomly, the dashboard will feel confusing. When they are arranged intentionally, the story becomes clear.

> [!alex]
> A good dashboard isn't just a data dump. If I need to communicate a story, I'll often use added notes along with my visuals to help people see the whole picture (if visuals alone aren't enough).

## What a Data Story Looks Like

Most effective data stories follow a simple flow.

## Start With the Big Picture

Begin with the most important takeaway. This is usually:

- A KPI
- A summary number
- A high-level trend

This answers the question, "What is happening right now?"

## Add Context

Once the main takeaway is clear, add visuals that explain why. These might show:

- Breakdowns by category
- Comparisons across regions
- Changes over time

> [!alex]
> A good dashboard feels like a conversation, not a dry report.

## Highlight the Impact

Good stories point to what matters most. Use visuals to:

- Call out problem areas.
- Show where performance is strong or weak.
- Focus attention on outliers.

> [!tip]
> Adding a text box next to a visual to provide additional context can be helpful when the visualization alone doesn't tell the whole story.

## Lead to Action

The best dashboards help someone decide what to do next. This might include:

- Filters to explore problem areas
- Supporting charts for deeper investigation
- Clear indicators of success or failure

## How Does This Relate to Us?

Think about our dashboard page:

1. **Big Picture**: The cards at the top show total revenue and units sold – the key metrics
2. **Context**: The area chart shows how revenue has been trending over time
3. **Breakdown**: The column charts show which stores and products drive the most engagement and revenue

questions.question: Which sequence best represents an effective way to tell a story with data on a dashboard?
answers: Start with the big picture, add context, then lead to action
Show all charts at once, then explain them with text
Begin with detailed tables, then summarize at the end
questions.answer: Start with the big picture, add context, then lead to action

# Formatting Dashboards

Formatting is what turns a dashboard from usable into professional. The data and charts might already be correct, but poor formatting can make everything harder to read and harder to trust.

_Good_ formatting usually isn't very noticeable – it's when it's bad that people start to notice.

> [!alex]
> If someone notices the formatting is off before anything else, there's a problem.

## Titles and Labels

Titles should explain what the viewer is looking at. Good titles:

- Describe the insight, not just the metric
- Are short and clear
- Match across similar visuals

Bad titles usually look like raw field names or technical terms.

## Alignment and Spacing

Clean alignment makes dashboards feel organized. In Power BI:

- Align visuals to each other.
- Keep spacing consistent.
- Avoid overlapping or crowded visuals.

White space can help separate ideas and improves readability.

## Assignment

# Legibility

Text should be easy to read from a distance. Try to:

- Use one font family.
- Keep similar visuals using the same text sizes.
- Make key numbers slightly larger than supporting text.

Small, inconsistent text is one of the most common dashboard issues.

2. [ ] Update the cards to show the comma separating the thousands place. Do this for each:
   - Select a card → Format your visual → General → Data format → Format options → Format → Whole number → toggle "thousands separator" _on_
3. [ ] Shrink the cards' sizes vertically, and grow the bottom 4 charts to take up some of the extra space.
4. [ ] Click on each visual and add a border: Format your visual → General → Effects → Visual Border -> `Yes`

lessons.title: Interactivity
lessons.readme:
# Interactivity

Interactivity is what separates static reports from real dashboards. Instead of just looking at data, users can click, filter, and explore on their own.

The goal is not to add as much interactivity as possible, but to add usefulness to the dashboard.

> [!alex]
> A good interactive dashboard lets someone answer follow-up questions without leaving the dashboard.

## Slicers

Slicers let users filter data without touching the underlying model. Common uses:

- Date ranges
- Regions
- Product categories

Slicers should be easy to find and clearly labeled. If a slicer exists, it should have a clear purpose.

## Cross Filtering and Highlighting

Power BI visuals interact with each other by default. When a user clicks one visual:

- Other visuals filter or highlight automatically
- Patterns and relationships become easier to spot

This is one of the most powerful features of Power BI and often requires no extra setup.

## Drill Down and Drill Through

Drill features allow users to move between levels of detail. _Drill down_ is useful for moving from:

- Year to month to day
- Category to subcategory

_Drill through_ lets users right-click a data point and navigate to a detailed page focused on that item.

> [!alex]
> Drill features are great, but only if users know they exist.

## Tooltips

Tooltips show extra information when users hover over a visual. They're useful for:

- Adding context without cluttering the dashboard
- Showing supporting metrics
- Providing definitions or explanations

Custom report page tooltips can add a lot of value when used carefully.

## Assignment

Let's add slicers to the Dashboard page so users can filter the data interactively.

1. [ ] Insert two Slicer visuals in the upper right corner where we left room.

   ![slicer icon](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/d7BEt2O-225x416.png)

2. [ ] Drag `dates[date]` to the Field of the first (top) Slicer.
3. [ ] Power BI should automatically display this as a date range slicer.
   > [!tip]
   > Date slicers with the "Between" style let users select a custom date range, which is great for exploring trends.
4. [ ] Drag `customers[customer_region]` to the Field of the second (bottom) Slicer.
5. [ ] Format the region slicer: Format your visual → Visual → Slicer settings → Options → Style → Tile
   > [!alex]
   > The "Tile" style makes region selection feel more like buttons, which is easier for users to understand at a glance.
6. [ ] Test the interactivity: click on a region tile and watch the other visuals update.
7. [ ] For consistency, add a visual border to the slicers as well.

![final](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/0insDcC-1280x720.png)

lessons.title: Filtering
lessons.readme:
# Filtering

Filtering controls what data people see when they open and interact with a dashboard. Good filtering makes dashboards feel focused. Bad filtering can make them feel confusing or broken – especially to people who haven't used filters before.

The idea is to show the right data by default while still allowing flexibility.

> [!alex]
> If users constantly have to fix filters, the dashboard is doing too much.

## Report-Level Filters

Report-level filters apply to every page in a report. These are useful when:

- The dashboard is meant for a specific audience.
- Certain data should never be shown.
- You want a consistent default view.

Examples include filtering to a single year or excluding test data.

## Page-Level Filters

Page-level filters apply only to the current page. These work well when:

- Different pages answer different questions.
- Each page focuses on a specific topic.
- You want control without affecting the entire report.

## Visual-Level Filters

Visual-level filters affect only one visual. These are helpful when:

- A chart needs a specific subset of data.
- You want to highlight top or bottom values.
- One visual should behave differently from others.

> [!alex]
> Visual-level filters are powerful, but easy to forget. Always document or label them clearly!

## Default Filter States

Filters are not just about interaction; they also define first impressions.

A dashboard should open in a clean, intentional state:

- No confusing filter combinations
- Clear default selections
- Predictable behavior when filters change

## Assignment

Let's apply different types of filters to understand how they work.

1. [ ] On the CEO Dashboard, ensure you can see the Filters pane (View → Filters).
2. [ ] Drag `sales[sale_discount]` to the "Filters on this page" section.
3. [ ] Set the filter to "is greater than" `0` and apply it.
   > [!info]
   > This page-level filter ensures the dashboard only shows discounted sales, which can be useful for analyzing promotion effectiveness.
4. [ ] Select the "Sales by Brand" clustered column chart.
5. [ ] In the Filters pane, find "Filters on this visual."
6. [ ] Go to Product Brand in the visual filter area.
7. [ ] Change the filter type to "Top N."
8. [ ] Set it to show Top 3 by `sale_quantity` and click "Apply filter."
   > [!tip]
   > Top N filters are great for focusing attention on what matters most without cluttering the visual with every category.
9. [ ] Click somewhere on the canvas (deselect the visual) to verify the page filter is still active.
10. [ ] Save the report.

> [!alex]
> Notice how the page-level filter (discounted sales only) affects all visuals, while the visual-level filter (Top 3 brands) affects only the clustered column chart. Understanding this hierarchy is key to building effective dashboards.

![final](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/FdmBQOb-1280x719.png)

lessons.title: Sharing and Publishing Dashboards
lessons.readme:
# Sharing and Publishing Dashboards

Once a dashboard is built, the next step is getting it in front of the right people. Dashboards are meant to be viewed, explored, and used to make decisions. If no one can access them, they don't provide much value.

## Power BI Desktop vs. Power BI Service

Power BI Desktop is where you build dashboards (it's what we've been using). [Power BI Service](https://app.powerbi.com/) is an online app where people can view and interact with them.

A typical workflow looks like this:

1. Build the report in Power BI Desktop.
2. Publish it to the Power BI Service.
3. Share it with others.

Most collaboration happens in the Power BI Service, not in Desktop.

## Publishing a Dashboard

To share a dashboard, it must be published. In this course, we're using the free Power BI Desktop version, which is great for building and learning, and unfortunately sharing reports through the Power BI Service requires a paid Power BI license. So we won't be doing it ourselves, but the process is simple if you want to in the future:

1. Open your report in Power BI Desktop.
2. Click Publish.
3. Choose a workspace.

Once published, the report becomes available in the Power BI Service and can be shared with others.

## Workspaces and Access

Workspaces are where reports and dashboards live in the Power BI Service. Common access roles include:

- **Viewer:** can view and interact with dashboards
- **Member:** can edit and publish content
- **Contributor:** can update content but with limited permissions

Choosing the right role helps to protect your work while still allowing collaboration.

> [!alex]
> Most users should be viewers. Editing access should be limited. (Personally, I don't want just anyone to change my dashboards that I've worked hard on.)

![Collaborating Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/collaborating-1920x1080.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

lessons.title: Scheduled Refreshes
lessons.readme:
# Scheduled Refreshes

As you know, you can click the "Refresh" button in the Home ribbon to refresh your data in Power BI Desktop. But when you publish your report to the Power BI Service, you can also set up an _automatic_ refresh schedule. This keeps your reports current without the need to manually open Power BI Desktop and click refresh.

## Why Scheduled Refreshes Matter

Dashboards are only useful if the data is current. Imagine a sales dashboard that shows last month's numbers when stakeholders expect to see yesterday's results. They'll lose trust in the dashboard quickly.

Scheduled refreshes solve this by automatically pulling fresh data at regular intervals.

> [!alex]
> Just remember, your data source must be accessible from the cloud for scheduled refreshes to work. If your data lives on a local file or behind a firewall, you'll need a data gateway.

## How to Schedule Refreshes

Again, you don't need to _do this now_. These steps happen in the **Power BI Service** in your browser, after publishing your report. But just so you know the process:

1. Open [Power BI Service](https://app.powerbi.com/) and go to the workspace containing your published report.
2. Select the report's **semantic model** from the workspace's content list.
3. On the semantic model's details page, select **Refresh → Schedule refresh**.
4. Configure the gateway connection and data source credentials if required. Our local CSV files would need a gateway so the Service could access them.
5. In the Refresh section, turn on **Configure a refresh schedule**, choose the frequency, time zone, and refresh times, then click **Apply**.

See Microsoft's [scheduled refresh guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/connect-data/refresh-scheduled-refresh) for more details.

## Common Refresh Frequencies

| Data Type                | Example Refresh Schedule                |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Frequently changing data | Every 30 minutes with Premium or Fabric |
| Daily sales data         | Once per day (overnight)                |
| Weekly reports           | Once per week                           |
| Historical analysis      | On-demand                               |

The available schedule depends on your license and capacity: Power BI Pro supports up to 8 scheduled refreshes per day; Premium per user and Premium/Fabric capacity support up to 48. Scheduled refresh is _not_ real-time, and refreshes can start somewhat later than their scheduled time.

lessons.title: Collaborating With Stakeholders
lessons.readme:
# Collaborating With Stakeholders

Building a dashboard is usually not the end of the process. Once people start using it, questions come up, feedback is shared, and changes are requested. This is where real collaboration begins.

## Gathering Feedback

Feedback is a good sign! It means people are engaged with the content and want to make it better.

Common types of feedback include:

- Requests for new metrics
- Questions about how numbers are calculated
- Suggestions to change layout or visuals

Try to understand the question behind each request. Often the real need is clarity, not another chart.

> [!alex]
> When someone asks for a new chart, I always ask "What decision will this help you make?" Sometimes the answer reveals they just need a filter on an existing chart.

## Iterating Without Breaking Things

Dashboards should evolve, but changes should be intentional. Good practices:

- Make small changes one at a time.
- Test updates before sharing again.
- Avoid constantly changing definitions of key metrics.

> [!alex]
> Frequent small improvements are better than constant redesigns. I recommend maintaining a stable version while working on updates.

## Setting Expectations and Boundaries

Not every request should turn into a dashboard change – it's usually a matter of clarification for the user, so they can understand how the dashboard works or what it shows.

It is okay to:

- Ask why a change is needed.
- Push back on unnecessary complexity.
- Explain tradeoffs clearly.

Clear communication helps prevent dashboards from becoming bloated and confusing. Remember, you're the expert, and you need to decide whether something gets added or not.

## Communicating Insights, Not Just Charts

When reviewing dashboards with stakeholders:

- Walk through the main takeaways.
- Explain what has changed since the last version.
- Highlight areas that need attention.

This helps ensure the dashboard leads to action, not just observation.
